request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 58 years
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: June 8, 2020
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted on June 8, 2020, due to increased oxygen requirements following a COVID-19 diagnosis.

Hospital Course:
The patient received high flow nasal cannula therapy on admission. However, on hospital day 6, mechanical ventilation (MV) was initiated due to respiratory distress, hypoxemia, and hypercapnia. Despite MV, the patient's respiratory failure continued to worsen. Therefore, venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) was implemented on hospital day 11. Meropenem, levofloxacin, convalescent plasma therapy, and dexamethasone were administered during the treatment course.

Outcome:
The patient showed gradual improvement in lung compliance and chest radiography. Ultimately, VV-ECMO was discontinued on hospital day 38.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient will continue to receive follow-up care and monitoring as required for complete recovery.
Primary Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]Secondary Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Co-Morbidities:
None

Procedures Performed:
MV and VV-ECMO were performed during hospitalization.

Medications Upon Discharge:
There were no medications prescribed at the time of discharge.

Recommendations:
The patient was advised to continue following a healthy lifestyle routine and receiving regular medical checkups.

Clinical Team:
- Attending Physician: [REDACTED]
- Nurse: [REDACTED]
- ECMO Specialist: [REDACTED]
- Respiratory Therapist: [REDACTED]
- Pharmacist: [REDACTED]
- Social Worker: [REDACTED]

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to rest and follow a healthy routine as per routine health guidelines. The patient was informed of follow-up appointments and instructed to contact the hospital in case of any concerns or queries.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: J12**

- **Principal condition:** The patient was admitted with COVID-19 lung disease. It caused worsening respiratory failure that needed mechanical ventilation and then VV-ECMO, and recovery was tracked through lung compliance and chest X-ray. That points to COVID-19 pneumonia as the condition chiefly responsible for the episode. Respiratory distress, hypoxaemia and hypercapnia are manifestations of it, not separate principal diagnoses.
- **Chapter letter:** J (respiratory system).
- **Category:** J12, viral pneumonia not elsewhere classified. At the fourth-character level this would be J12.8, other viral pneumonia.
- **Why not a COVID code as principal:** COVID-19 confirmed by testing has its own code, U07.1. My understanding of Australian coding guidance is that the respiratory manifestation is sequenced first, with U07.1 added as an additional diagnosis. This should be checked against the current Australian Coding Standards for your edition.
- **Uncertainty:** The diagnosis section is withheld and the summary never states "pneumonia" outright, so J12 is an inference from the clinical picture. If the clinician documented acute respiratory distress syndrome as the main condition, J80 could apply instead.
